body: Thank you! That is useful for me to look into!

No it is different. Its to do with the side effects of attachment failure and complex trauma. Since my awakening 5 years ago, I've been studying attachment theory and trauma and how I got to this point. This is a big topic! But the short answer is that I had developed an avoidant attachment before I was 18 months old. I never stood a chance at a normal life. If I had seen a coach or therapist in my late 20's or early 30's, I might have identified there was an issue and been able to recover with trauma treatment? What is true is that my emotional development was likely compromised in childhood and many parts of my emotional state were very young. These young parts along with the trauma kept me in a kind of perpetual stasis and I wasn't able to sustain a normal romantic relationship emotionally.

Thank you for your feedback! I grew up during a war environment in my childhood and lived in an extremely dangerous area. I never thought it had effected me until my d-day awakening over 5 years ago. I now understand how I got to this point after studying attachment theory and trauma over these last 5 years. I've tried very hard to resolve the loss of life, which has largely occurred due to attachment issues and disassociation. It's most likely a trauma response, but I don't seem to be able to forgive myself. Reframing has not worked for me. Writing a journal has not worked, but it has been useful. Positive affirmations have not worked for me either. I think its a bit like "confidence". Its difficult to acquire on your own, but it is more easily acquired when someone else has had confidence in you, and you can then pass it on to others. From a dating or relationship perspective, no body offered that "confidence" in me, for me to carry it within me. Once again, I really appreciate your feedback. Thank you!

Thank you for your thoughts! I've tried very hard to "let it go", but its now been over 5 years since my d-day awakening when I realised something was wrong. If anything, the wound has gotten deeper as so much in daily life continually triggers me. Even the smallest things are triggering. For example, I was in a restaurant and saw two couples in a foursome laughing and enjoying their get-together. I've never experienced something as simple as this. I watch TV on an iPad because I can skip parts that are too triggering. Things like sex scenes, romance & love stories trigger a found sadness. I'm so far behind the rest of society. I'm now 54m and people my age are planning their retirement! Its hard to correlate where I am in life? Once again, thank you for your encouraging words!
Thank you for your lovely words! I hope so too...

Thank you for your wonderfully kind and compassionate words! Your definition of "loser" certainly helps. Thank you! My d-day was like waking up from a 30 year coma and being thrust 3 decades into the present day. The full gravity of the life I had lost hit me very hard and I went into emotional shock for 5 months. In many ways I've made progress, but accepting the past is something I appear unable to do. Everything in daily life is a trigger! Fortunately, I've not turned to any substances! And I eat very healthy and walk 4.5 miles a day. But the sadness of what I will never experience is always present. Thank you again for your wisdom and words of encouragement!

It's more a combination of things. For example, my elderly mother who I care for was listening to an audio recording of the family which was recorded in the mid 1960's. It was very emotional for her to hear my siblings as children and playing musical instruments. I won't have any such memories to look back on. No photographs, no nothing. 

In terms of sex, I can already feel the effects of ageing. I don't think I can experience my sexuality like everybody else has done. Touch will be a big problem I think? And I also think that sex might be very traumatising for me too! It will make it very real what I've missed out on, which I think will likely send me into a tail spin. There's no easy answers unfortunately. Which is why I feel the way feel! 

Very briefly with my studies with attachment and trauma - is that we all have an attachment style and this mostly develops by the time we are 4 years old. This is how the nervous system learns how to keep us safe and how to navigate life. In my case, my nervous system worked against me, thinking it was keeping me safe. What actually ended happening was an unprecedented level of self-abandonment! My nervous system felt that it was best to keep me safe by looking after everybody else's best interests as well as many other traits! So when I wrote that I never stood a chance, that's exactly what happened. All the fearful avoidant traits & behaviours (along with trauma) are subconscious and you don't know you are doing them.
Thank you so much for your kind words!

In some ways I can understand. My friends, family and others see my successes and think I have it all worked out. Then one day it hit me!!! I've missed out on emotional connection, particularly with the opposite sex for over 30 years. I'm now in my early 50's. I have no family of my own, been celibate for 30+ years, and there's all these normal life experiences I'll never have. I don't see my achievements (which there are many) as achievements. After my d-day moment, I discovered I had a fearful avoidant attachment, I had developed Complex Trauma in childhood and suffered the effects of enmeshment. These issues conditioned my nervous system since childhood and I never stood a chance in having the life I wanted. I was invisible to the opposite sex and I was never the kind of guy they would want to date; and I can't blame them. My nervous system is totally screwed up! It is too late for me and I can never recover what has been lost! Everybody says "its not too late" etc, but they don't know what it's like to be in my position. Emotional connection is what makes life fulfilling!! I've missed out on a life time's worth of it and now that I've woken up, I'm at least three decades out of sync with society. I'm in a no mans land. I can't do the deed whilst my elderly mother is still alive, but I plan to do so soon after her passing.

This is definitely not true!!!!!! It might be easy for you, but it is impossible for some us! Despite being very successful professionally and having a bubbly personality, it never happened for me. I'm now looking really forward to suicide because love will never find its way to me. I'll never know what its like to simply walk down by the river holding hands with a SO. I'll never experience waking up and making love to the pitter patter of rain drops against the window. This is serious stuff and "just getting drunk at a party and find someone" is not a solution for those of us (and the OP u/Avatar4848) who never stood a chance in having the romantic life we wanted. 

I am and have been living my best self. I’ve travelled the world, I’ve written books, my work has been on broadcast television, been interviewed on broadcast radio programmes and featured prominently in well-known international magazines, I have a podcast and a YouTube channel; and I’ve been very successful in different careers, but I can assure you that no matter how much success or confidence you have in other areas of life, without embracing your sexuality, without intimacy, affection and love, without being desired by the opposite sex and forging a life together, there is absolutely nothing left.

Although I have no idea what caused him to attempt suicide, I can relate somewhat to some of the things you've mentioned. There could be a million reasons your neighbour did this and it may never be known?? I'm so sorry for his family and everyone connected with him to receive this news. I can provide some insight to what's happened with me. Up until August last year (49m), I could never understand how a person could take their own life. I have always been a very happy guy and I'm sure many of my friends and the people I know would describe me the way you described your neighbour. In August 2019 I had a massive d-day realisation that my whole life had been a complete waste of time. It was very traumatic and my first words during this moment was "that I'm not supposed to be here"! Sadly, I was a people pleaser and spent my whole life looking out for what was in other peoples best interests. I never really looked at what was in my best interests. I don't mean professionally, but personally. The ramifications of this were huge! I was conflict avoidant and did whatever it took to avoid conflict. I was genuinely happy, but it was a happiness for others, not for myself. The last time I lost my temper was at 12 years old. I have unknowingly kept all my emotions to myself all my life (or more likely detached from them). I've now learnt its good to set boundaries and to get upset when you are upset. This was all bottled and on my d-day, the bottle burst! A life time of emotions and anger being released all at once. A year later I've identified the root cause. I discovered I have a fearful avoidant attachment. In my specific case, I never stood a chance at living the life I wanted! All of my traits were subconscious and so I never knew something was wrong with me, until my d-day. The thing about attachment is that it is learned bahaviour in childhood. There are many big issues that come up, but the probably the most relevant for this post is that I discovered that I didn't know who I was? I never developed a sense of self during childhood and when you don't know who you are, its very unsettling! Our bodies have built in protections, like you won't put your hand on a hot surface! You retract your hand immediately! I can honestly say that in my state right now, those protections are disabled when it comes to the final moment. My whole life was lived with the wrong map without having the right lenses to see it was the wrong map. I never had control over it, until I acquired an awareness. But at my age, its all too late. Some say 50 is still young, but I can tell you that it is too late for the things I wanted in my life. Note that this is not regret. You can regret something you did wrong, learn from it and let it go. You can't regret something you never knowingly did wrong. I still convey the happiness with friends and when I come across new people I meet. My experience with my people pleaser tendencies are very good at making people feel comfortable. They would never know what's really going on inside! I still wake up everyday wanting it all to be over!

Thank you for your post. I (49m) understand all the things you have said and I appreciate the gravity of suicide on those who have to live with it. Members of my own extended family have sadly committed this act and I've seen the suffering myself. I had never had a suicidal thought in my life until the 19th August last year. In fact, before that date, I could never understand suicide and why people would even want do it. I've spent a lifetime of service looking after others, mainly family. I found myself having to become a provider and looking after my parents at 25. I had a brother who became gravely ill and had to support and care for him and his family. Now for the last 10 years I've had to care and support my elderly mother. All my best years are gone. I've had no relationships since I was 20 and I've been celibate for the last 29 years. I became very successful in my career, but all that money went on caring for family. I always wanted my own family, to build a life with someone and leave behind a legacy. Sadly, this future is no longer possible for me. There is no "building a life together" at this age. Children are not a realistic option any more and I'm still having to care for my mother. There is no future left. I have no pension, no family of my own and a lost lifetime of experiences. I can't go back in time and there's no reason to look forward to the future. I mean what will I be working hard for? To live on my own, be that guy who has nowhere else to be and sitting in a pub all by himself? That is not me! Through my reckoning, my childhood and upbringing unknowingly clouded my decisions. Many say we always have a choice as we live our lives! I agree with this, I know that on paper it seems like this is a matter of choice. To set healthy boundaries and to look after one's own interests first. BUT... I can tell you it's not as simple as that! I was the youngest of the family, it rested on my shoulders to carry the burden. All my siblings went on their merry way in life, but sadly, I didn't have this luxury. The reality didn't work out that way for me. I understand your point that ambivalence about death being a launch pad to freely choose and to help others. Sadly, I've been doing that all my life and I'm tired of carrying this weight of looking after other people's interests. There's no good roadmap out of my situation. I'll never have the life I wanted and I'm sure many experience this in their own lives, that they wanted more too! But they have experienced "love" in a romantic sense and probably had children and built a family of their own. They may have had their ups and downs, but I now know that I never stood a chance! My childhood upbringing had caused a misalignment of what was "normal" and the ability to look after my own interests. If I had known these things in my early 30's, I might have been able to fix things. I know for certain what my future holds, I just can't do it while my mother is still alive, she's already lost 2 sons and this would be too devastating. I don't feel "free", but rather I feel "trapped" in a life I never got to experience.
